title: Significant Economic Risk
description: Significant economic risk has two uses under IRC Section 41: contract research payment contingency and the internal use software innovation test.
summary: Significant economic risk is a U.S. R&D tax credit concept under IRC Section 41 with two distinct uses: for taxpayers performing contract research, credits depend on whether payment is contingent on research success and they retain substantial rights; for internal use software, it requires committing substantial resources amid heightened technical uncertainty about recovering them within a reasonable period.

body.text: Significant economic risk is a U.S. R&D tax credit concept under IRC Section 41 with two distinct uses: for taxpayers performing contract research, credits depend on whether payment is contingent on research success and they retain substantial rights; for internal use software, it requires committing substantial resources amid heightened technical uncertainty about recovering them within a reasonable period.

Significant economic risk operates across two legally distinct inquiries under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41), and conflating them distorts how research and development (R&D) tax credit eligibility is evaluated. For contract and grant research generally, IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d) (26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)) exclude research from qualified research to the extent it is "funded" by another person or governmental entity, turning on whether the performing taxpayer retains substantial rights in the research and whether payment is contingent on the success of the research—meaning the performer bears the financial risk of failure. Separately, for internal use software (IUS) under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E), "significant economic risk" is a specific regulatory term of art inside the three-part High Threshold of Innovation (HTI) test codified at 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C), requiring the commitment of substantial resources alongside a heightened degree of technical uncertainty over whether those resources can be recovered within a reasonable period.

Second, in administrative compliance, IRS Form 6765 Instructions (Rev. December 2025) mandate Section G business-component reporting for tax years beginning after 2025 (subject to the 80%/Top 50 business components rule), while an updated Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) directive (ts-21-0126-0032, effective January 2, 2026, amending IRM 21.7.4.4.8.3.5(16)) sets January 10, 2027 specifically for perfecting amended-return refund claims and formally waives two formerly required individual-level items for claims postmarked June 18, 2024 and subsequent.
Foundational Statutory and Regulatory Architecture
Resolving the Regulatory Conflation Between Funded Research and Internal Use Software

The statutory origin of the funded research exclusion is IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H), which excludes from the definition of "qualified research" any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. Because IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) does not statutorily define the term "funded," the operative regulatory framework resides in 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d). Although 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A carries a historical section heading referencing "Qualified research for taxable years beginning before January 1, 1986," 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(e)(1) and 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(9), together with uniform federal appellate and Tax Court enforcement, expressly apply 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d) to determine whether research performed for another person in current tax years is funded. According to June and July 2026 legal commentary from KPMG TaxNewsFlash, Miller & Chevalier, and Current Federal Tax Developments analyzing Smith, et al. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (June 16, 2026), Judge Weiler squarely rejected a post-Loper Bright challenge seeking to invalidate 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d), holding that decades of Federal Circuit, Court of Federal Claims, and Tax Court decisions validating the regulation's "contingent on success" and "substantial rights" requirements remain binding under statutory stare decisis and that the regulation independently merits respect under Skidmore based on its longevity, consistency, and clarity.

By contrast, 26 CFR Section 1.41-4—which was promulgated under Treasury Decision (T.D.) 9104 (2004-6 I.R.B.) and generally applies to expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003—governs the four-part qualified research test under IRC Section 41(d)(1) (including the requirement that activities be undertaken to eliminate uncertainty concerning capability, method, or appropriate design through a process of experimentation) and houses the specialized internal use software rules in 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6), whose final version under T.D. 9786 (81 FR 68306, 2016-42 I.R.B.) is effective for taxable years beginning on or after October 4, 2016. That framing merges two legally distinct inquiries: 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d) asks whether a contract researcher's payment is contingent on the success of the research and whether the performer retains substantial rights in the results, whereas 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C) measures resource-recovery uncertainty solely to determine whether software developed primarily for internal general and administrative use overcomes the statutory exclusion in IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E).

That statement reverses the regulation on its face. Under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(1), "[a]mounts payable under any agreement that are contingent on the success of the research and thus considered to be paid for the product or result of the research (see § 1.41-2(e)(2)) are not treated as funding". For the performing researcher, payment contingency shifts the financial risk of failure onto the performer, preserving unfunded status if substantial rights are also retained. Conversely, 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(e)(2) operates on the paying customer's side of a third-party contract research agreement: an expense is paid or incurred for the performance of qualified research on behalf of the customer only to the extent it is paid or incurred pursuant to an agreement that (i) is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, (ii) provides that the research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer, and (iii) requires the customer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful. If payment by the customer is contingent on the success of the research, 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(e)(2) specifies that the customer's payment is considered paid for the product or result rather than the performance of research, disqualifying that contingent portion from the customer's contract research expenses—as illustrated in Example 4 of 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(e)(5), where Taxpayer A reimburses Corporation B $200x unconditionally and pays an additional $100x only if the research succeeds, limiting Taxpayer A's eligible contract research expense to $130x (65% of the non-contingent $200x).

cells: General Funded Research Exclusion (Performer Side)
Is payment contingent on the success of the research, and does the performing taxpayer retain substantial rights in the research?
Research is treated as funded to the extent of non-contingent payments under § 1.41-4A(d)(3) (or 100% fully funded under § 1.41-4A(d)(2) if no substantial rights are retained).
Contract Research Expense Eligibility (Customer Side)
Did the customer enter into the agreement prior to performance, is the research performed on the customer's behalf, and must the customer bear the expense even if the research fails?
Customer cannot treat contingent product purchases as contract research expenses (normally eligible at 65%, or 75%/100% under statutory enhancements).
Internal Use Software Significant Economic Risk
Are substantial resources committed with heightened technical uncertainty at project inception that those resources will be recovered within a reasonable period?
Internal use software fails the High Threshold of Innovation (HTI) test and is excluded from the research credit (unless a dual-function subset or safe harbor applies).

body.text: Dual Criteria of the Funded Research Exclusion and Substantial Rights

Under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d), contract research avoids funded status completely only when two independent requirements are met concurrently across all agreements (not merely formal research contracts) entered into between the performing taxpayer and other persons. First, under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(1), amounts payable to the researcher are excluded from funding only if they are contingent on the success of the research. Second, under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(2) and (d)(3)(i), the performing taxpayer must retain "substantial rights" in the research. Furthermore, under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(3)(iii), the funded-research rules must be applied separately on a project-by-project basis to each research project undertaken by the taxpayer. Where a customer seeks to claim contract research expenses, 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(e)(2)(i)—as highlighted by the Federal Circuit in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995)—also mandates that the research agreement be entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, reflecting Congress's design of the credit as an ex ante investment incentive.

If the performing taxpayer retains no substantial rights in the research—for instance, because an agreement "confers on another person the exclusive right to exploit the results of the research" under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(2) or requires the performing taxpayer "to pay for the right to use the results of the research" under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i)—the research is "treated as fully funded" and none of the performer's expenditures constitute qualified research expenses. The regulation explicitly provides that incidental benefits to the taxpayer from performing the research, such as increased experience or general technical know-how in a field of research, do not constitute substantial rights in the research. As summarized in The Tax Adviser's analysis of substantial-rights case law, in Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), the Federal Circuit held that retaining a non-exclusive right to use the research results in the contractor's own business without paying the customer for that right satisfies the substantial-rights standard, rejecting the government's contention that a researcher must hold the exclusive right to exclude others. Conversely, in Dynetics, Inc. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015), and Grigsby v. United States, No. 19-00596-BAJ-SDJ (M.D. La. Oct. 19, 2022), federal courts held that contractors lacked substantial rights where military security restrictions (DD Form 254) or broad contractual clauses ("work for hire," transfers of "all rights, title, and interest," or requirements to obtain prior client consent before reusing project data) stripped the performer of an autonomous legal right to reuse the research results.

Moreover, the final sentence of 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(2) creates an explicit regulatory gap in which neither party to a contract may claim the R&D tax credit: "If a taxpayer performing research for another person retains no substantial rights in the research and if the payments to the researcher are contingent upon the success of the research, neither the performer nor the person paying for the research is entitled to treat any portion of the expenditures as qualified research expenditures". In that scenario, the performer is disqualified under Section 1.41-4A(d)(2) for lacking substantial rights, while the paying customer is simultaneously disqualified under Section 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii) because its payment was contingent on success and thus paid for a finished product rather than for the performance of research.

While commercially common, that inverse correlation is not automatic under federal tax law—as demonstrated both by the dual-disqualification trap in 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(2) and by the four partially funded architectural contracts analyzed in Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50, where legal commentary notes that the architecture firm retained substantial rights via copyright retention or reuse licenses even though payments were not contingent on research success. Additionally, two specialized provisions in 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(4) and (d)(5) govern government contracting and multi-year timing: under paragraph (d)(4), independent research and development (IR&D) costs and bid and proposal (B&P) costs allocated to government contracts under the Federal Acquisition Regulations (FAR) System are not treated as funding the underlying research activities except to the extent properly severable from the contract; and under paragraph (d)(5) (illustrated in Example 5 of paragraph (d)(6)), if a taxpayer cannot determine the extent to which research is funded at the time its return is filed, the taxpayer must initially treat the research as completely funded and subsequently file an amended return once the final funding amount is determined.
Judicial Precedent Allocating Financial Risk of Research Failure
Fairchild Industries and the Financing-Versus-Funding Distinction

The foundational appellate precedent governing financial risk under the funded research exclusion is Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. Nov. 29, 1995), modified February 23, 1996, reversing 30 Fed. Cl. 839 (1994). In July 1982, Fairchild entered into a fixed-price incentive contract with the U.S. Air Force to design and produce the T-46A "Next Generation Trainer" aircraft. The contract's Full-Scale Development (FSD) phase carried an amended ceiling price of $133,485,885 and required Fairchild to design, build, test, and deliver two prototype aircraft and support systems under a "Total System Responsibility" clause governed by over 1,000 pages of detailed technical specifications. Between 1982 and 1986, Fairchild spent $216,056,000 on the FSD phase. Under the contract's bimonthly financing provisions governed by Defense Acquisition Regulations (DAR) 7-104.35(a), the Air Force disbursed progress payments calculated as a percentage of incurred costs, but under DAR 7-104.35(h) those progress payments remained unliquidated, refundable advances (legally analogous to loans secured by inventory under Marine Midland Bank v. United States) until specific contract line items were delivered and formally accepted under DAR 7-302.2. After Congress canceled the T-46A program in late 1986, a termination-for-convenience audit determined that Fairchild had successfully completed 90% of the FSD work, entitling Fairchild to $120.6 million ($53.0 million in previously liquidated progress payments, $60.8 million in unliquidated progress payments credited against the termination settlement, and a $6.8 million final cash payment), leaving Fairchild with over $95 million in unrecovered FSD research costs. Applying predecessor IRC Section 44F(d)(3) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-5(d)(1) (which contained the identical "contingent on the success of the research" standard now codified in 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(1)), the IRS disallowed 55.8% ($50.3 million, representing the ratio of the $120.6 million paid by the Air Force to the $216.1 million total FSD costs) of Fairchild's $89.8 million in net claimed QREs (out of $109.4 million originally reported less $19.6 million disallowed on unrelated grounds), revoking $5.8 million in research tax credits for tax years 1983 and 1984.

The Court of Federal Claims ruled for the government on the theory that Fairchild received regular bimonthly progress payments and expected to be paid for its work. Writing for a unanimous Federal Circuit panel, Circuit Judge Newman reversed and remanded, drawing a foundational distinction between "funding" under the statute and the mechanics of interim contract financing. The Federal Circuit held that the inquiry under the regulation "turns on who bears the research costs upon failure," not on the ex ante likelihood of technical success or on post-hoc observation that the contractor ultimately succeeded and was paid. Because the contract's quality assurance and inspection procedures (DAR 7-302.2 and 7-302.4) required item-by-item Air Force evaluation against over 1,000 pages of strict technical specifications and empowered the Air Force to reject unacceptable work, compel Fairchild to correct defects at its own expense, accept non-conforming work at an equitable price reduction, or require full repayment of unliquidated progress payments upon default, Fairchild's legal right to retain any payment remained genuinely "contingent on the success of the research". The court also rejected the government's "wait and see" argument that research credits should depend on whether a contract proves unprofitable at completion, explaining that Congress enacted the research credit as an upfront investment incentive whose availability must be determinable from the contractual allocation of risk before funds are committed.
Geosyntec Consultants and the Rejection of Cost-Overrun Risk

In Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015) (opinion by Circuit Judge Wilson), affirming No. 12-80334-Civ (S.D. Fla. Apr. 15/17, 2013), a specialized environmental and geological infrastructure engineering firm sought a federal income tax refund of $1,677,432 under 26 U.S.C. § 41 for tax years 2002 through 2005. To resolve the funded-research issue across hundreds of client engagements, the parties designated six representative contracts for summary judgment review: three fixed-price contracts and three cost-plus capped contracts. The district court held that the three fixed-price contracts were unfunded (a ruling the IRS conceded and settled for a refund of $255,575 plus statutory interest) because their milestone inspection and acceptance clauses allowed clients to withhold payment until each milestone was completed and accepted. However, the district court held that the three cost-plus capped contracts were funded, and Geosyntec appealed two of those capped contracts to the Eleventh Circuit: the Cherry Island Contract with the Delaware Solid Waste Authority (DSWA) to expand landfill capacity in Wilmington, Delaware (capped at approximately $10 million with additional sub-caps), and the WM Contract with Waste Management, Inc. to evaluate groundwater remediation technology beneath a warehouse in Niagara, New York.

In reality, the Eleventh Circuit flatly rejected Geosyntec's cost-overrun theory and affirmed summary judgment for the United States, holding both capped contracts fully funded and completely ineligible for the credit. Under both contracts, Geosyntec billed monthly for labor and expenses incurred on pre-defined tasks at pre-defined rates plus a markup, subject to an agreed-upon maximum ceiling price. Addressing Geosyntec's contention that it bore financial risk because cost overruns above the ceiling would eliminate its profit and force it to absorb excess performance costs, the Eleventh Circuit held verbatim: "Cost-of-performance is not the financial risk with which we are concerned because 'the only issue is whether payment was contingent on the success of the research'—that is, the financial risk of failure". Moreover, the court noted that under the Cherry Island Contract, Geosyntec was explicitly entitled to an "equitable adjustment of its compensation" or "extra compensation" if state environmental regulators (DNREC) imposed unreasonable demands requiring extra work or if mandatory public hearings caused costs to exceed subtask totals.

The Eleventh Circuit also rejected Geosyntec's argument that client invoice-review rights, dispute resolution clauses, and professional standard-of-care obligations placed economic risk on the contractor. Distinguishing Fairchild's 1,000-page item-by-item technical acceptance regime, the Eleventh Circuit drew a bright line between "proper performance" of professional engineering services and successful research outcomes. Under both the Cherry Island and WM contracts, monthly invoices were payable upon submission, and while the clients could temporarily withhold disputed amounts for accounting inaccuracies or alleged professional negligence, Geosyntec remained legally entitled to payment for executing its assigned tasks according to ordinary professional standards even if its bench tests or remediation evaluations failed to yield a viable technical solution for the client. Because the clients—not Geosyntec—bore the financial loss if properly performed research failed to achieve the desired technical result, both capped contracts were funded under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d).
Smith v. Commissioner and the June 2026 Merits Ruling

That December 18, 2024 procedural order merely denied the Commissioner's motion for summary judgment because genuine issues of material fact remained regarding how the underlying contracts operated across the firm's international projects.

On June 16, 2026, following trial, Judge Weiler issued the U.S. Tax Court's merits opinion in Adrian D. Smith and Nancy W. Smith, et al. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50, as detailed in published legal and accounting analyses from KPMG TaxNewsFlash, Miller & Chevalier, Grant Thornton, Massie Tax Credits, and Current Federal Tax Developments. As those analyses report, the case involved Adrian Smith, Carlisle Gill, and Robert Forest, the sole partners of Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture, LLP (AS+GG), an Illinois limited liability partnership specializing in sustainable "supertall" buildings and masterplans whose design work integrated architecture, structural engineering, mechanical engineering, fluid dynamics, microclimates, thermodynamics, and geotechnics. AS+GG claimed Section 41 credits for the 2008, 2009, and 2010 tax years across 48 projects, which the parties stipulated to try using six representative international sample projects: Atrium City Tower, Kingdom Tower, Plot 14, Masdar HQ, Atrium City Masterplan, and Plot R2. Prior to trial, the IRS conceded that all sample projects satisfied the four-part qualified research test under IRC Section 41(d)(1) and the exclusions under Section 41(d)(4)(A)–(G), as well as asserted penalties, leaving two substantive issues for decision: whether the six sample projects were excluded as "funded research" under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d), and whether compensation and guaranteed payments deducted and included in 2008 partner wage QREs were reasonable under IRC Section 174(e).

First, on the administrative law challenge, Miller & Chevalier and Current Federal Tax Developments report that the taxpayers argued under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024), that Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d) was invalid because its two-pronged test was not the "single best reading" of IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H), urging the Tax Court to replace the regulation with a dictionary definition of "funded" as "a sum of money set apart for a specific objective". Judge Weiler rejected the challenge on two independent grounds: quoting Loper Bright's express limiting language on statutory stare decisis, the Tax Court held that prior decisions of the Federal Circuit, the Court of Federal Claims, and the Tax Court upholding and applying Section 1.41-4A(d) remain binding precedent, and further determined that Section 1.41-4A(d) independently warrants Skidmore deference because its decades-old framework provides consistency, clarity, and certainty.

Second, on payment contingency under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(1), the taxpayers relied on Fairchild to contend that payments on all six sample projects were contingent on research success because the contracts required client approval at the end of each design phase or milestone before payments were released. As KPMG, Grant Thornton, and Miller & Chevalier note, Judge Weiler rejected that argument, aligning the Tax Court's analysis with the Eighth Circuit's decision in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. May 6, 2024) (affirming T.C. Memo. 2022-127, where a Minnesota structural engineering firm lost approximately $190,000 in R&D credits across fiscal years ending September 30, 2010, 2011, and 2013 because phase inspections, code-compliance duties, and termination-for-nonperformance clauses did not tie payment to the technical success of the research). Judge Weiler distinguished between "successful performance" (satisfying rigid, detailed technical specifications like the 1,000+ pages in Fairchild) and "proper performance" (delivering architectural designs under a general professional standard of care free from negligence, defects, or errors). Because AS+GG billed on hourly rates or percentage-of-completion schedules tied to project phases rather than objective technical success metrics—and because potential loss of future profit under termination clauses does not constitute research failure risk—none of the six sample projects had payments contingent on the success of the research under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(1).

Third, evaluating substantial rights on a project-by-project basis under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(2) and (d)(3), the Tax Court split the six sample projects into two groups. For two sample projects (Kingdom Tower and Plot 14), the contracts explicitly transferred copyright to the clients, made all project data the "absolute property" of the clients, and required AS+GG to obtain "express prior written approval" (which the clients had unlimited discretion to withhold) before reusing any project information. Rejecting the taxpayers' attempt to invoke foreign copyright laws of the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom to override the explicit contract text, the Court held that Kingdom Tower and Plot 14 were 100% funded and completely ineligible under Section 1.41-4A(d)(2). However, for the remaining four sample projects (Atrium City Tower, Masdar HQ, Atrium City Masterplan, and Plot R2), AS+GG retained copyrights or negotiated licenses permitting the firm to reuse and market the underlying research without paying the clients. Partially striking down the IRS's complete disallowance, Judge Weiler held that those four projects were partially funded under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(3), entitling the partners to claim R&D credits to the extent AS+GG's otherwise qualified research expenses for each project exceeded the payments received from the client, and directed the parties to apply a pro-rata portfolio resolution across the remaining unexamined projects. Finally, on the secondary issue under IRC Section 174(e), because an appeal in Smith would lie to the Seventh Circuit, Judge Weiler applied the Seventh Circuit's "independent investor test" (Exacto Spring Corp.) under the Golsen rule; because the IRS's own expert witness admitted that a hypothetical independent investor in AS+GG would have realized a 939% return on equity after paying the partners' compensation, the Tax Court sustained the 2008 partner wage QREs in full.
Contractual Risk Allocation Mechanisms and Worked Hypotheticals
Risk Distribution Across Standard and Hybrid Contract Structures

Contractual payment terms and intellectual property clauses are the primary determinants of which party bears the financial risk of research failure, although judicial decisions from Fairchild to Geosyntec, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, and Smith emphasize that contract labels alone are never dispositive. Time-and-materials (T&M) and cost-reimbursable contracts (illustrated in federal procurement commentary on FAR Part 16 by cost-plus-fixed-fee [CPFF] and cost-plus-award-fee [CPAF] agreements) ordinarily assign financial risk to the customer because the contractor is compensated for hours worked and allowable costs incurred regardless of whether the research succeeds. As Geosyntec confirms, capped cost-plus contracts are likewise treated as funded whenever the researcher receives cost-based reimbursement up to a ceiling price without an express or clearly implied technical-success contingency.

As the Eighth Circuit held in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), and the Tax Court reaffirmed in Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50, a fixed-price or phased-milestone contract avoids funded status under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(1) only if the contract terms expressly or by clear implication condition the contractor's right to receive or retain payment on the successful outcome of the research itself (measured against specific, objective technical criteria rather than general professional standards of care), AND the contractor concurrently retains substantial rights under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(2). Where an agreement provides non-contingent funding (such as milestone or fixed payments not conditioned on technical research success) but the performing researcher retains substantial rights in the research results, 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i) treats the research as partially funded and reduces the performer's otherwise qualified research expenses dollar-for-dollar by the funding received, unless the taxpayer establishes eligibility for pro-rata allocation between qualified and nonqualified research expenses under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii).

headers: R&D Tax Credit Eligibility Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)

cells: Fixed-Price With Technical Acceptance
Performer bears direct financial loss if technical specifications or prototypes fail acceptance.
Payment (or right to retain unliquidated progress advances) is conditioned on meeting specific technical specifications and formal client acceptance (Fairchild).
Unfunded under § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and eligible for performer in full, provided performer also retains substantial rights under § 1.41-4A(d)(2).
Fixed-Price or Milestone Without Success Contingency
Performer bears general budget or cost-overrun risk, but client bears research failure risk.
Fixed or milestone fee is payable for delivering professional services or phase deliverables under a standard of care without detailed technical-success criteria (Meyer, Borgman & Johnson; Smith).

Treated as funded under § 1.41-4A(d)(1); completely ineligible if no substantial rights are retained, or eligible only to the extent QREs exceed client payments under § 1.41-4A(d)(3) if substantial rights are retained (Smith).
Time and Materials (T&M)
Customer pays for labor hours and materials expended regardless of technical outcome.
Billed hourly or per unit of material as work progresses without a technical-success condition.
Funded for the performer; customer may evaluate claiming 65% (or 75%/100%) contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2) if research is performed on its behalf.
Cost-Reimbursable (e.g., CPFF / CPAF)
Customer reimburses all allowable incurred costs regardless of success.
Guaranteed reimbursement of actual incurred expenses plus a fixed or award fee (see 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(5) Ex. 3 & 4).
Funded and ineligible for performer (unless QREs exceed total payments received while retaining substantial rights); non-contingent portion is eligible for customer under § 1.41-2(e)(2).
Capped Cost-Plus
Customer bears research failure risk up to the cap; performer bears only cost-of-performance overrun risk above the cap.
Monthly cost-plus reimbursement up to a maximum ceiling price not conditioned on technical research success.
Held fully funded and ineligible for the performer under Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015).
Partially Funded Grant or Contract (With Substantial Rights)
Shared only when performer's total research expenditures exceed non-contingent customer funding.
Non-contingent grant or contract funding covers only a portion of the performer's total research expenditures.

Performer retaining substantial rights may claim excess QREs via § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i) dollar-for-dollar offset or § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii) pro-rata allocation (subject to the mandatory 65% funding offset floor).

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Examples of Contractual Risk Transfer

In Hypothetical Example 1 (Fixed-Price Contract Contingent on Objective Technical Specifications), suppose Taxpayer A enters into a $500,000 fixed-price contract with Client B prior to performance to develop a proprietary electric-vehicle battery electrolyte required to achieve a minimum specific energy density of 500 Wh/kg. Under the explicit terms of the contract, Client B holds the right to test the prototype against the 500 Wh/kg benchmark, reject a non-conforming prototype, and withhold the entire $500,000 contract price if the 500 Wh/kg specification is not achieved; concurrently, Taxpayer A retains non-exclusive substantial rights to manufacture, license, or use the underlying electrolyte technology in its own business without paying Client B. During the tax year, Taxpayer A incurs $400,000 in internal qualified research expenses (engineering wages and laboratory supplies). If Taxpayer A's experimentation resolves the technical uncertainty, achieves 500 Wh/kg, and passes Client B's acceptance testing, Taxpayer A collects the $500,000 contract price, recovers its $400,000 QREs, realizes a net positive margin of $100,000 ($500,000 contract revenue − $400,000 internal QREs = $100,000), and treats all $400,000 as unfunded QREs under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(1) because payment was contingent on technical success at project inception (while Client B cannot treat any portion of its $500,000 contingent payment as a contract research expense under 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(e)(2)). Conversely, if unresolved technical uncertainty limits the prototype's energy density to 450 Wh/kg and Client B rejects the prototype, Taxpayer A receives $0 in revenue and absorbs a direct net financial loss of $400,000 ($0 revenue − $400,000 internal QREs = −$400,000) caused by technical failure—satisfying 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(1) under Fairchild. However, if Taxpayer A had granted Client B exclusive ownership of all research results or required Client B's discretionary consent to reuse the technology as in Smith (Kingdom Tower and Plot 14), 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(2) would disqualify all $400,000 of Taxpayer A's QREs even though payment was contingent on achieving 500 Wh/kg.

Under Scenario A (Time-and-Materials Hourly Billing), DevShop contracts to perform AI research and development billed monthly at $200 per hour regardless of whether the AI works; after expending 1,000 hours, even if the research fails completely, DevShop collects $200,000 (1,000 hours × $200/hour = $200,000) and suffers $0 in unrecovered financial exposure to failure, rendering DevShop's work 100% funded and ineligible under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(1). Provided the agreement was executed prior to performance, the research was performed on the client's behalf (meaning the client has a right to the research results under 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(e)(3)), and the underlying work satisfies IRC Section 41(d)(1), the client may evaluate treating 65% of the non-contingent payment—$130,000 (0.65 × $200,000 = $130,000)—as a qualified contract research expense under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A) and 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(e)(1)–(2). Under Scenario B (Fixed Bid Contingent on Technical User Acceptance Testing [UAT]), DevShop agrees to a $200,000 flat fee payable solely upon passing technical UAT while retaining non-exclusive substantial rights. If resolving technical uncertainties consumes 2,000 engineering hours (representing $200,000 in internal QREs at an illustrative internal cost of $100/hour, or $400,000 at a $200/hour billing equivalent) and the software fails UAT, DevShop receives $0 and absorbs 100% of its internal costs. Under Fairchild, Geosyntec, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, and Smith, however, the UAT criteria in the contract must test concrete, measurable technical specifications resolving technological uncertainty rather than general commercial satisfaction or routine professional standards of care.

Under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i), when a performing taxpayer retains substantial rights in the research, non-contingent funding ordinarily reduces the taxpayer's otherwise qualified research expenses dollar-for-dollar. However, under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii), if the taxpayer establishes to the satisfaction of the district director (A) the total amount of research expenses, (B) that total research expenses exceed the funding, and (C) that the otherwise qualified research expenses (expenses that would be QREs if there were no funding) exceed 65% of the funding, the taxpayer may allocate the funding pro rata between nonqualified research expenses (such as overhead) and otherwise qualified research expenses—subject to the strict floor that "[i]n no event, however, shall less than 65 percent of the funding be applied against the otherwise qualified research expenses". In Example 1 of 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(6), where Corporation B retains substantial rights, receives $120x in unconditional funding from Customer A, and incurs $150x in total research expenses ($100x in-house QREs, $40x outside contract research of which $26x is an otherwise QRE at 65%, and $10x overhead, totaling $126x in otherwise QREs), the default dollar-for-dollar rule leaves $6x ($126x − $120x = $6x), whereas pro-rata allocation applies $100.8x of funding ($120x × [$126x / $150x] = $100.8x, exceeding the 65% floor of $78x) to yield $25.2x in eligible QREs ($126x − $100.8x = $25.2x); in Example 4, where $20x of the $120x payment is contingent on producing a useful product, only the $100x unconditional payment is treated as funding, reducing the pro-rata offset to $84x ($100x × [$126x / $150x] = $84x) and leaving $42x in eligible QREs ($126x − $84x = $42x). Similarly, if Taxpayer C retains substantial rights, receives $100,000 in non-contingent funding, and incurs $200,000 in total research expenses composed of $160,000 in otherwise QREs and $40,000 in nonqualified expenses, otherwise QREs ($160,000) exceed 65% of funding ($65,000); pro-rata allocation offsets 80% ($160,000 / $200,000 = 80%, or $80,000) of the funding against otherwise QREs, leaving $80,000 in eligible QREs ($160,000 − $80,000 = $80,000) instead of $60,000 under the dollar-for-dollar rule ($160,000 − $100,000 = $60,000). By contrast, if Taxpayer C's $200,000 in total expenses consisted of $100,000 in otherwise QREs and $100,000 in nonqualified expenses, a raw 50% ratio ($50,000) would violate the 65% floor, forcing a minimum offset of $65,000 (0.65 × $100,000 = $65,000) and leaving $35,000 in eligible QREs ($100,000 − $65,000 = $35,000).
Significant Economic Risk Under the Internal Use Software High Threshold of Innovation Test
Scope of the IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E) Exclusion and Statutory Carveouts

IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E) generally excludes from qualified research any activity with respect to computer software that is developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use by the taxpayer, except to the extent provided in regulations. Final regulations promulgated under T.D. 9786 (81 FR 68306, 2016-42 I.R.B.; codified at 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6) and effective for taxable years beginning on or after October 4, 2016, with optional reliance on either the 2015 proposed regulations [REG-153656-03] or the final regulations for tax years ending after January 20, 2015 and beginning before October 4, 2016, as noted in The Tax Adviser) narrow the definition of "primarily for internal use" to software developed for use in "general and administrative functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business" (including software developed primarily for the internal general and administrative use of a related party treated as a single taxpayer under IRC Section 41(f)). Whether software is developed primarily for internal use depends on the taxpayer's intent and the facts and circumstances at the beginning of the software development. Under T.D. 9786, general and administrative functions are strictly limited to three categories: (1) financial management functions (financial management and supporting recordkeeping, including accounts payable, accounts receivable, inventory management, budgeting, cash management, cost accounting, disbursements, economic analysis and forecasting, financial reporting, finance, fixed asset accounting, general ledger bookkeeping, internal audit, management accounting, risk management, strategic business planning, and tax); (2) human resources management functions (managing the workforce, including recruiting, hiring, training, assigning personnel, maintaining personnel records, payroll, and benefits); and (3) support services functions (supporting day-to-day operations, including data processing, facility services such as groundskeeping, housekeeping, janitorial, and logistics, graphic services, marketing, legal services, government compliance services, printing and publication services, and security services such as video surveillance and physical asset protection from fire and theft).

Software falls outside the internal use restriction (or is exempted from the High Threshold of Innovation test) if it satisfies specific statutory or regulatory carveouts under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E) and 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6): (a) software developed for internal use in an activity that independently constitutes qualified research (other than the development of the internal use software itself); (b) software developed for internal use in a production process that meets the requirements of IRC Section 41(d)(1); (c) a new or improved package of software and hardware developed together by the taxpayer as a single product (or modifications to an acquired software-hardware package) of which the software is an integral part used directly by the taxpayer in providing services in its trade or business, which is evaluated together as a single combined product; and (d) software that is not developed for general and administrative functions, including software developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties, as well as software developed to enable a taxpayer to interact with third parties or to allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system.

For dual-function software—defined in 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(A) as software developed both for use in general and administrative functions and to enable a taxpayer to interact with third parties or allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system—the regulation establishes a presumption that the software is developed primarily for internal use. However, under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B), to the extent a taxpayer can identify a discrete subset of software elements that only enables third-party interaction or allows third parties to initiate functions or review data (a "third party subset"), that third-party subset is exempted from the internal use presumption and is not developed primarily for internal use. Furthermore, under the dual-function safe harbor in 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C), if dual-function software (or a remaining "dual function subset" after carving out any third-party subset) remains, the taxpayer may include 25% of the qualified research expenditures of that dual-function software or subset in computing the Section 41 credit without satisfying the HTI test, provided that (1) the research activities otherwise constitute qualified research under IRC Section 41(d) (without regard to Section 41(d)(4)(E)), and (2) the dual-function software's or subset's use by third parties (or by the taxpayer to interact with third parties) is reasonably anticipated at the beginning of development to constitute at least 10% of its total use, estimated using an objective, reasonable industry method such as processing time, amount of data transfer, or number of user interface screens. Example 14 of 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii) illustrates this mechanism: where Taxpayer X incurs $50,000 of research expenditures on dual-function software, identifies a third-party Subset A accounting for 50% ($25,000) of the expenditures, and reasonably anticipates that third-party usage of the remaining dual-function Subset B ($25,000) will account for 15% of total processing time (exceeding the 10% threshold), X may include all $25,000 allocable to Subset A plus $6,250 (25% × $25,000 = $6,250) of Subset B's expenditures under the safe harbor. Where software remains classified as internal use software (and outside the third-party subset or 25% safe harbor), it qualifies for the R&D tax credit only if the taxpayer establishes all three prongs of the High Threshold of Innovation (HTI) test under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A): (1) the software is innovative, (2) the software development involves significant economic risk, and (3) the software is not commercially available for use by the taxpayer without modifications that would satisfy both the innovation and significant economic risk requirements.
Heightened Uncertainty and the Appropriate Design Nuance

Under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C), internal use software development involves significant economic risk only "if the taxpayer commits substantial resources to the development and if there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period". Crucially, the regulation explicitly commands: "The term 'substantial uncertainty' requires a higher level of uncertainty and technical risk than that required for business components that are not internal use software". As the regulation further explains, this standard does not require technical uncertainty regarding whether the final result can ever be achieved, but rather whether the final result can be achieved within a timeframe that will allow the substantial resources committed to the development to be recovered within a reasonable period. Technical risk must arise from uncertainty that is technological in nature as defined in 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(a)(4), and "substantial uncertainty must exist at the beginning of the taxpayer's activities".

Example 16 in T.D. 9786 (2016-42 I.R.B.) demonstrates how strictly this resource-recovery timeframe standard operates in practice: where a taxpayer commits substantial resources to rewrite a legacy mainframe application using an object-oriented programming language on a client/server platform to achieve substantial improvements in speed and cost reductions, and faces methodology uncertainty under the general four-part test, the project nonetheless fails the significant economic risk prong of the HTI test if, at the outset of development, the taxpayer is confident that it can overcome the technological uncertainties and recover its committed resources within a reasonable period.

In the January 2015 proposed regulations (REG-153656-03), Treasury and the IRS had proposed restricting "substantial uncertainty" in the regulatory text exclusively to uncertainty regarding capability or method, excluding uncertainty regarding appropriate design. Following public comments pointing out that IRC Sections 174 and 41 have long recognized design uncertainty and that capability, method, and design uncertainties overlap in software engineering, the final 2016 regulations in T.D. 9786 removed that categorical textual exclusion from 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C), shifting the regulatory focus from the type of uncertainty to the heightened level of uncertainty. At the same time, Treasury and the IRS cautioned in the T.D. 9786 preamble (2016-42 I.R.B.) that because adding the modifier "substantial" before "uncertainty" establishes a higher threshold than the ordinary four-part test, internal use software research activities involving only appropriate design uncertainty (and no capability or methodology uncertainty) will rarely satisfy the substantial uncertainty requirement—while recognizing that "the appropriate design uncertainty of internal use software may be inextricably linked to substantial uncertainty regarding capability or method".
Interplay With Innovation and Commercial Availability Prongs

Within the three-part HTI architecture of 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii), the significant economic risk prong operates in tandem with the innovation and non-commercial-availability prongs. Under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(B), software is "innovative" if it would result in a reduction in cost, an improvement in speed, or another measurable improvement that is "substantial and economically significant, if the development is or would have been successful". The regulation expressly specifies that this is a "measurable objective standard, not a determination of the unique or novel nature of the software or the software development process" (rejecting an older, more restrictive "unique or novel" test). Under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(D), application of the HTI test takes into account only the results anticipated to be attributable to the development of the new or improved software at the beginning of the software development, independent of the effect of any modifications to related hardware or other software. The regulation further clarifies that the implementation of existing technology by itself is not evidence of innovation, but the use of existing technology in new ways can serve as evidence of a high threshold of innovation if it resolves the heightened "substantial uncertainty" required by paragraph (c)(6)(vii)(C).

Finally, under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(3), the software must not be commercially available for use by the taxpayer, meaning the software "cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would satisfy" both the innovation requirement of paragraph (c)(6)(vii)(A)(1) and the significant economic risk requirement of paragraph (c)(6)(vii)(A)(2).
Substantiation, Procedural Compliance, and 2026–2027 Disclosure Deadlines
Third-Party Contract Expenditure Rules and Recordkeeping Basis

When a taxpayer pays or incurs expenses to a non-employee to conduct qualified research on the taxpayer's behalf under contract terms where the taxpayer bears the financial risk of failure (meaning payments are not contingent on success under 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(e)(2)), IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A) generally limits eligible "contract research expenses" to 65% of the amount paid or incurred. Where a contract calls for both qualified services and other services, 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(e)(1) limits the 65% inclusion strictly to the portion of the amount paid or incurred attributable to qualified research or services that, if performed by employees of the taxpayer, would constitute qualified services within the meaning of IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B). Under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(B) and 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(e)(4), if any contract research expense paid or incurred during a taxable year is attributable to qualified research to be conducted after the close of that taxable year, that prepaid amount is treated as paid or incurred during the subsequent period in which the qualified research is actually conducted.

IRC Section 41(b)(3)(C) and (D) provide two statutory rate enhancements that replace the standard 65% limitation on Form 6765. First, under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(C), a 75% rate applies to amounts paid or incurred by the taxpayer to a "qualified research consortium" for qualified research conducted on behalf of the taxpayer and one or more unrelated taxpayers (treating all persons aggregated as a single employer under IRC Section 52(a) or (b) as related), where a qualified research consortium is defined under Section 41(b)(3)(C)(ii) as any organization described in IRC Section 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(6) that is exempt from tax under Section 501(a), is organized and operated primarily to conduct scientific research, and is not a private foundation. Second, under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(D), a 100% rate applies to amounts paid or incurred by the taxpayer for qualified research that is energy research performed by (I) an eligible small business (defined in clauses (ii) and (iii) as a business employing an annual average of 500 or fewer employees during either of the two preceding calendar years in which the taxpayer does not own, within the meaning of IRC Section 318, 50% or more of the voting power/value of stock or capital/profits interests), (II) an institution of higher education (as defined in IRC Section 3304(f)), or (III) a Federal laboratory (as defined in Section 4(6) of the Stevenson-Wydler Technology Innovation Act of 1980, 15 U.S.C. § 3703(6)).

Specifically, 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(d), titled Recordkeeping for the research credit, provides verbatim: "A taxpayer claiming a credit under section 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. For the rules governing record retention, see § 1.6001-1". Under 26 CFR Section 1.6001-1(a), any person subject to income tax under subtitle A of the Internal Revenue Code "shall keep such permanent books of account or records, including inventories, as are sufficient to establish the amount of gross income, deductions, credits, or other matters required to be shown by such person in any return of such tax or information," and under 26 CFR Section 1.6001-1(e), such books or records "shall be kept at all times available for inspection by authorized internal revenue officers or employees, and shall be retained so long as the contents thereof may become material in the administration of any internal revenue law". As the T.D. 9104 preamble (2004-6 I.R.B.) explains, Treasury and the IRS intentionally declined to mandate a rigid, one-size-fits-all checklist of specific contemporaneous documents in 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(d) beyond the general substantiation requirements of IRC Section 6001 and 26 CFR Section 1.6001-1. However, because 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(1) requires evaluating "[a]ll agreements (not only research contracts) entered into between the taxpayer performing the research and other persons" and because the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) requires documentation of cost centers, qualifying wages, supplies, contract research expenses, and excluded activities, substantiating unfunded status or pro-rata allocation under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii) in practice requires retaining the complete contractual record—including master service agreements, statements of work, change orders, technical specifications, invoicing schedules, and project-level cost accounting ledgers.
Refund Claim Specificity After Harper and Premier Tech

That framing misstates the judicial outcome of both cases: as documented in analyses by The Tax Adviser, Miller Canfield, and CLA, the taxpayers actually prevailed against the government's specificity motions in both Harper and Premier Tech, and it was the government's litigation losses in those two cases that prompted the IRS to overhaul its administrative intake rules for research credit refund claims. Under IRC Section 7422, a taxpayer may not maintain a federal court suit for a tax refund until a claim for refund has been duly filed according to the provisions of law and Treasury regulations, and under 26 CFR Section 301.6402-2(b)(1), a refund claim must set forth in detail each ground upon which a credit or refund is claimed along with facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis thereof.

In Harper v. United States, No. 19-55933 (9th Cir. Feb. 25, 2021), as summarized in The Tax Adviser, Jeffrey Harper, the sole shareholder of military design-build contractor Harper Construction Co. (HCC), filed amended returns in 2012 claiming Section 41 R&D credits of $437,632 for 2008 and $388,325 for 2010 that initially stated only that they were reporting credits for increasing research activity without attaching supporting factual narratives. Rather than rejecting the forms at intake, the IRS conducted a four-year substantive audit, issuing questions and reviewing over 100,000 pages of supporting documentation before denying the claims on the merits on September 12, 2016 and instructing Harper to file suit in district court. When Harper sued, the government moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under 26 CFR Section 301.6402-2(b)(1), and the district court dismissed the action. The Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded, holding under Supreme Court precedent (Angelus Milling Co. v. Commissioner, 325 U.S. 293 (1945)) that the IRS's four-year substantive examination and merits determination constituted a "textbook case of waiver" of the formal specificity requirements of Section 301.6402-2(b)(1). A concurring Ninth Circuit judge added that while administrative exhaustion under IRC Section 7422 is jurisdictional, the regulatory formatting rules in 26 CFR Section 301.6402-2(b)(1) are non-jurisdictional and had been satisfied and perfected under the informal-claim doctrine.

Similarly, in Premier Tech, Inc. v. United States (D. Utah July 15, 2021), as summarized by Miller Canfield and CLA, the government moved to dismiss a taxpayer's R&D credit refund suit on the ground that the taxpayer's amended return failed 26 CFR Section 301.6402-2(b)(1) by omitting granular project-by-project and employee-by-employee details. On July 15, 2021, the U.S. District Court for the District of Utah flatly denied the government's motion, holding: "the United States offers no authority for imposing such a requirement. Form 6765 does not ask taxpayers to provide any of these details. If the IRS wants more information about the research tax credits, the IRS could require that information on Form 6765. It does not, and the IRS cannot now say its own forms are not sufficient to constitute claims for refunds. That would lead to absurd and patently unfair results for taxpayers". Directly in response to its defeats in Harper and Premier Tech—and to prevent substantive examinations from waiving specificity objections while answering the Utah district court's observation about Form 6765—the IRS on October 15, 2021 issued Information Release IR-2021-203 and Office of Chief Counsel Field Attorney Advice Memorandum 20214101F, directing IRS intake classifiers to screen amended-return Section 41 refund claims before any audit begins and summarily reject ("No Consider") claims that failed to provide five specific project-level data items upfront (prohibiting "data dumps" unless exact page locations were cited), followed by the structural redesign of Form 6765 itself.
Form 6765 Section G Mandate and the January 10, 2027 Perfection Window
Official IRS guidance separates these two compliance tracks into distinct regimes with different effective dates and rules.

First, for original and general return filings governed by Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024) and the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), completing Section G (Business Component Information) is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless filing an amended return) and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025, subject to Section G reporting guidelines. Filers must first indicate in Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary) whether they are required to complete Section G. When Section G is required, filers must report individual business components under the "80% / Top 50" rule—identifying business components that account for at least 80% of total QREs, up to a maximum of 50 business components—and report any remaining business components on a single line labeled "Aggregate Business Components" in column 49(c) (entering aggregate dollar totals across columns 50 through 56 while leaving other descriptive columns blank). For each reported business component, the taxpayer must categorize the component in column 49(d) (Product, Process, or All Others) and, if the business component is software, classify it on line 49(e) using the mandatory IRS software codes: Category A (IUS) for internal use software developed primarily for general and administrative functions subject to the three-part HTI test; Category B (DFS — Dual Function Software), subdivided into B.1 (no third-party subset identified and safe harbor not applied), B.2 (third-party subset identified, leaving the remaining dual-function subset subject to the HTI test), and B.3 (25% safe harbor applied where anticipated third-party usage is at least 10%); Category C (Excepted from IUS Treatment), subdivided into C.1 (software for use in an activity that constitutes qualified research), C.2 (software for internal use in a qualifying Section 41(d)(1) production process), and C.3 (new or improved combined hardware-software package); or Non-IUS for software not developed for general and administrative functions (such as software sold, leased, licensed, or marketed to third parties or enabling third-party interaction). Across Columns 50 through 56 of Section G, the filer must disaggregate QREs for each business component into Column 50 (in-house wages for actual conduct of research), Column 51 (in-house wages for direct first-line supervision, excluding higher-level managers), Column 52 (in-house wages for direct support, excluding general administrative support), Column 53 (total wages, carried to Section F, line 42), Column 54 (supplies, carried to Section F, line 43), Column 55 (off-premises computer rental/lease costs where the taxpayer is not the operator or primary user, carried to Section F, line 44), and Column 56 (contract research expenses at 100%, 75%, or 65%, carried to Section F, line 45).

Second, specifically for amended income tax returns (Forms 1120X, 1040X, and amended Forms 1041) involving Section 41 research credit refund claims filed between January 10, 2022, and January 10, 2027, IRM 21.7.4.4.8.3.5(16) (updated via IRS Procedural Update ts-21-0126-0032, effective January 2, 2026) grants taxpayers a formal perfection period. Under the January 2, 2026 IRM revision, while five items were originally required prior to June 18, 2024, effective for claims postmarked/dated June 18, 2024 and subsequent, the IRS formally waived the requirements to provide (4) the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and (5) the information each individual sought to discover. Consequently, for amended-return refund claims postmarked on or after June 18, 2024, taxpayers must provide three mandatory items at the time the claim is filed: (1) identify all the business components to which the Section 41 research credit claim relates for that year; (2) for each business component, identify all research activities performed; and (3) provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year. Under IRM 21.7.4.4.8.3.5(16), if an amended return filed during the perfection window (through January 10, 2027) omits any required item, IRS classifiers request Accounts Management (AM) to issue Letter 6426C (or Letter 916C), suspending the case and granting the taxpayer 45 days to respond via fax. If the taxpayer responds, the case is re-suspended to CAT-A for classifier review; if the taxpayer fails to respond after 60 days, or if the response fails to meet the required criteria, Accounts Management issues Letter 6424C (No Consider), rejecting the refund claim without substantive examination.
Regulatory Ambiguities, Section 174/174A Alignment, and Compliance Analysis
Gaps in Guidance and Harmonization With Research Expenditure Capitalization

Primary review of 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C) and T.D. 9786 confirms that neither "substantial resources" nor "reasonable period" carries a numeric dollar threshold, percentage-of-revenue safe harbor, or fixed month/year recovery period in the regulations, leaving both determinations dependent on a taxpayer's specific facts and circumstances at project inception.

Issued in September 2023 to provide interim guidance on specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures under post-TCJA IRC Section 174, IRS Notice 2023-63 (2023-39 I.R.B. 919) explicitly states that the notice "is not intended to change the rules for determining eligibility for or computation of the research credit under § 41 and the regulations thereunder (including rules for 'research with respect to computer software' and the definitions of 'qualified research' and 'qualified research expenses')". For a research provider (the contractor performing the work), as summarized in tax-practice commentary on Section 6.02 of Notice 2023-63, "financial risk" is defined as "the risk that the research provider may suffer a financial loss related to the failure of the research to produce the desired SRE product," while an "SRE product" is defined in Section 6.02(4) as any pilot model, process, formula, invention, technique, patent, computer software, or similar property (or component thereof) subject to protection under applicable domestic or foreign law (excluding mere unprotected know-how gained through performing research services).

Crucially, Section 6.04 of Notice 2023-63 created a structural asymmetry between Section 41 and Section 174 for contract research providers. Under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d), a contractor can claim the Section 41 research credit only if it both bears financial risk (payment contingent on success) and retains substantial rights (and only one party can claim the Section 41 credit for any one dollar of cost). By contrast, under Section 6.04 of Notice 2023-63, a research provider's costs are treated as SRE expenditures under Section 174 if the provider either bears financial risk under the contract or holds an "SRE product right" (a right to use any resulting SRE product in its trade or business or otherwise exploit it through sale, lease, or license, unless that right is available only upon obtaining approval from an unrelated party to the research arrangement). As illustrated in Section 6.05 of Notice 2023-63 (where Company C pays contractor Company D a $25,000 fixed sum plus reimbursement of $125,000 in actual development expenditures [$150,000 total] with no performance guarantees and no right for Company D to use or exploit the resulting SRE product, so Company D's $125,000 is not an SRE expenditure under Section 174 while Company C's $150,000 is treated as an SRE expenditure under Section 6.03), if a contractor does not bear financial risk (making its work funded and ineligible under Section 41) but does retain a right to use or exploit the resulting SRE product, the contractor's costs are nonetheless treated as SRE expenditures under Section 174. Recognizing that Section 6.04 of Notice 2023-63 could improperly require a research provider that does not bear financial risk to capitalize costs when obtaining only incidental contract-performance rights, Treasury and the IRS issued Notice 2024-12 (2024-5 I.R.B. 616, released December 22, 2023, effective retroactively to September 8, 2023 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021). Section 3 of Notice 2024-12 modifies Section 6.04 of Notice 2023-63 to clarify that if a research provider does not bear financial risk under the contract and obtains only an "excluded SRE product right"—defined as either (1) an SRE product right that arose from consideration other than the cost paid or incurred by the research provider to perform SRE activities under that contract (a separately bargained-for right), or (2) an SRE product right acquired for the limited purpose of performing SRE activities under that contract or another contract with the research recipient (a limited-purpose right)—and obtains no other SRE product right under the contract, then the provider's costs are not SRE expenditures.

Furthermore, on July 4, 2025, Congress enacted Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 193, H.R. 1), Title VII, Section 70302 of which added 26 U.S.C. § 174A (Domestic research or experimental expenditures) to the Internal Revenue Code. As codified in 26 U.S.C. § 174A and explained in tax-practice analyses, mandatory 5-year capitalization and amortization is repealed for domestic research or experimental expenditures (including software development under Section 174A(d)(3), while excluding land/depreciable property under Section 174A(d)(1) and mineral exploration under Section 174A(d)(2)), restoring current deductions under Section 174A(a) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 (with an optional election under Section 174A(c) to capitalize and amortize domestic R&E expenditures over not less than 60 months). Under the statutory transition rules in Section 70302(f) of P.L. 119-21 and implementing IRS procedural guidance (Rev. Proc. 2025-08 and Rev. Proc. 2025-28), (1) eligible small businesses meeting the IRC Section 448(c) gross receipts test for the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 were granted a one-year window through July 4/6, 2026 to elect retroactive application of Section 174A back to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 via amended returns (accompanied by late IRC Section 280C(c)(2) reduced-credit election or revocation relief), and (2) taxpayers could elect to recover remaining unamortized domestic SRE amounts capitalized during 2022–2024 either in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 or ratably over the two-taxable-year period (2025 and 2026) on a cut-off basis without IRC Section 481(a) adjustments. However, foreign research or experimental expenditures remain subject to mandatory 15-year midpoint amortization under amended IRC Section 174 (with post-May 12, 2025 disposition, retirement, or abandonment deductions barred under Section 70302(b)(1)(C)(ii) of P.L. 119-21, and with Section 6 of Notice 2023-63 continuing to be relied upon for foreign R&E expenditures as noted in secondary commentary citing Rev. Proc. 2025-23 § 7.03(1)(a) as modified by Rev. Proc. 2026-32 § 3.04). Despite Notice 2024-12 and the 2025 procedural updates, no unified final regulations harmonizing Section 41 financial-risk standards with Section 174/174A contract-research rules appear in the consulted IRS guidance.

cells: "Substantial Resources" and "Reasonable Period" for IUS SER
Governed by a subjective facts-and-circumstances standard at project inception under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C) with no quantitative safe harbors or numeric recovery-period thresholds.
Alignment Between IRC § 41 SER and § 174 / § 174A Contract Risk

Notice 2023-63 disclaims altering § 41 rules; Notice 2024-12 carves out "excluded SRE product rights" for non-risk-bearing contractors; P.L. 119-21 § 70302 enacted 26 U.S.C. § 174A restoring domestic expensing after 2024 while retaining 15-year amortization under § 174 for foreign research; no final unified regulations issued.
Complex and Hybrid Contract Risk Attribution

Geosyntec (776 F.3d 1330) holds capped cost-plus contracts without technical success contingencies are 100% funded; Meyer, Borgman & Johnson (100 F.4th 986) and Smith (T.C. Memo. 2026-50) hold milestone/fixed-price contracts without specific technical acceptance criteria are funded, though Smith allows partial-funding excess QRE claims under § 1.41-4A(d)(3) where substantial rights are retained.

body.text: Analytical Recommendations for Contract Structuring and Audit Preparation

items: Pre-Execution Contract Risk and Intellectual Property Reviews: Before qualified research begins—satisfying the pre-performance agreement requirement of 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(e)(2)(i) noted in Fairchild for third-party contract research expenses and establishing the ex ante allocation of risk upfront—tax and legal counsel should review Master Service Agreements, Statements of Work, and change orders against both prongs of 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d). For contractors seeking to claim unfunded QREs, the agreement must preserve non-exclusive substantial rights to reuse the research results in the contractor's business without paying the client or requiring discretionary client consent (avoiding the copyright-transfer and prior-written-approval disqualifications in Smith [Kingdom Tower and Plot 14], Dynetics, and Grigsby), and explicitly tie the right to receive or retain milestone and fixed payments to measurable, objective technical specifications and formal acceptance testing (as in Fairchild) rather than general professional standards of care or percentage-of-completion progress (which failed in Geosyntec, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, and Smith). Where a contractor does not bear financial risk and wishes to avoid unwanted Section 174/174A capitalization complexities on funded service contracts, counsel should ensure any license to client IP is drafted strictly as a "limited-purpose right" to perform the contract (an "excluded SRE product right" under Section 3 of Notice 2024-12).

Contemporaneous Technical Uncertainty and Economic Risk Memoranda: To satisfy the substantiation standards of 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(d) and 26 CFR Section 1.6001-1(a)–(e), taxpayers should prepare project-inception memoranda that document the specific technological uncertainties (capability, methodology, or inextricably linked appropriate design) existing at the beginning of the taxpayer's activities. For contract research, these records should map technical acceptance criteria directly to forfeitable payment milestones under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(1)—or, where the taxpayer retains substantial rights under a non-contingent contract as in the four partially funded projects in Smith, track project-by-project total research expenses, otherwise qualified research expenses, and total client payments to substantiate excess QREs under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i) or pro-rata allocation above the 65% floor under Section 1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii)—while strictly separating technical failure risk from general cost-overrun exposure rejected in Geosyntec. For internal use software under 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C), project-inception documentation should quantify the committed development budget ("substantial resources"), the anticipated economic recovery timeline ("reasonable period"), and why heightened technical uncertainty (beyond routine appropriate design) threatens recovery within that timeframe—or, for dual-function software under Section 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B)–(C), document the architecture of any third-party subset and the objective metric (such as processing time or data transfer volume) establishing at least 10% third-party usage for the 25% safe harbor.

Integration With Form 6765 Section G and the January 10, 2027 Perfection Window: Taxpayers should configure project-accounting and time-tracking systems to capture QREs by individual business component across Columns 50 through 56 of Form 6765—satisfying Section G's mandatory post-2025 "80% / Top 50" reporting threshold and Line 49(e) software category classifications (IUS, DFS [B.1, B.2, B.3], Excepted [C.1, C.2, C.3], and Non-IUS) under the December 2025 Form 6765 Instructions. For any pending or planned amended-return refund claims (Forms 1120X, 1040X, or amended Forms 1041), taxpayers should ensure that the initial filing includes all three active mandatory specificity items required by IRM 21.7.4.4.8.3.5(16) (ts-21-0126-0032, effective January 2, 2026) for claims postmarked June 18, 2024 and subsequent—(1) all business components, (2) all research activities performed for each business component, and (3) total qualified employee wage, supply, and contract research expenses—and respond to any IRS Letter 6426C or Letter 916C within the 45-day window prior to the January 10, 2027 perfection cutoff to avoid a final Letter 6424C (No Consider) disallowance.
